```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 80)
library(metamicrobiomeR)
options(metamicrobiomeR.quiet = TRUE)
```

Studies of the same question are often done on different platforms: a 16S study of one region, another of a
different region on a different sequencer, a shotgun study. They use different databases, name taxa differently,
and sequence to very different depths. A **combined analysis** merges the raw tables and fits one model; it needs a
table the studies share. A **meta-analysis** analyses each study on its own terms and combines the *estimates*;
it only needs the estimates to be comparable. This vignette runs both on the simulated `example_studies`
(four studies on three platforms, with six genera given a known difference, see `?example_studies`) and compares them.

## What the studies share

```{r check}
check_poolable(example_studies, rank = "genus")
```

The 16S studies hold ASVs and the shotgun study holds genera, with different naming (`[Eubacterium]`, `Blautia_A`).
Names are matched across databases, so most genera appear in several studies, but only some in all four.

## Meta-analysis: each study on its own, then pool

```{r meta}
res <- meta_analyse(example_studies, ~ group + age, term = "groupcase", rank = "genus", engine = "lm_asin",
                    fit_args = list(longitudinal = FALSE))
two <- as.data.frame(res)
c(genera = nrow(two), significant_at_5pct = sum(two$p_adjust <= 0.05))
```

## Combined analysis: merge the tables, adjust for study

`merge_studies()` matches taxa by name and keeps the genera present in every study (the default), and the model adjusts
for the study:

```{r combined}
merged <- merge_studies(example_studies, rank = "genus")
one <- fit_study(merged, ~ group + age + study, engine = "lm_asin", longitudinal = FALSE)
one <- one[one$term == "groupcase", ]
one$p_adjust <- p.adjust(one$p_value, "fdr")
c(genera = nrow(one), significant_at_5pct = sum(one$p_adjust <= 0.05))
```

## What differs

```{r compare}
both <- merge(two[, c("feature", "estimate")], one[, c("feature", "estimate")], by = "feature", suffixes = c("_meta", "_combined"))
c(genera_in_both = nrow(both), correlation_of_estimates = round(cor(both$estimate_meta, both$estimate_combined), 2),
  share_with_same_sign = mean(sign(both$estimate_meta) == sign(both$estimate_combined)))
setdiff(two$feature, one$feature)              # genera only the meta-analysis can use
head(two[order(two$p_value), "feature"], 5)    # strongest genera, meta-analysis
head(one[order(one$p_value), "feature"], 5)    # strongest genera, combined analysis
```

* **The estimates agree.** For the genera both analyses use, the effects are almost the same, and the strongest genera
  are the same (four of the five strongest are planted differences).
* **Coverage differs.** The combined analysis can only use genera present in every study; the meta-analysis uses every
  genus seen in at least two studies, including some the merge drops.
* **Significance differs a lot.** The combined analysis has 200 samples and calls most genera significant, but only six
  were given a true difference: most of the rest shift a little because relative abundances are compositional (when
  some genera rise, the others fall), and with high power small shifts become "significant". The meta-analysis, with
  four studies, is conservative and finds none at the default test. **Neither count is the answer**: look at effect sizes,
  their consistency across studies, and the heterogeneity (`summary(res)`).

## Which to use?

| | Combined analysis | Meta-analysis |
|---|---|---|
| Needs a shared feature table | yes | no |
| Needs raw data from every study | yes | no: estimates are enough (`effects_from()`) |
| Genera analysed | those in every study | those in at least two |
| Power with a few studies | higher | lower: the default test is conservative |
| Shows how much studies disagree | no | yes: I2, prediction intervals |
| Handles batch differences | with a study term | within each study |

When you can do both, report both: agreement strengthens the conclusion, and a difference tells you where to look.
When the raw data cannot be merged or shared, the meta-analysis is the way to combine them.
